episodes.summary_en: Hoya travels back to Joseon to learn why King Sejong created 28 new letters in 1443, and how the book Hunminjeongeum explained them in 1446.
learning_goals: Say who created Hangeul (King Sejong, the fourth king of Joseon) and when (1443).
Explain in one sentence why King Sejong made new letters: so ordinary people could learn them easily and write what they wanted to say.
Know that the book Hunminjeongeum (1446) explained the new letters, with explanations written by Jiphyeonjeon scholars.
Read and say 세종대왕, 한자, 훈민정음, 백성, 집현전 and 한글 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya the tiger opens a glowing storybook. Whoosh! We land in Joseon, Korea, almost 600 years ago. Here lived King Sejong, the fourth king of the Joseon dynasty.
scenes.illustration: Hoya, a friendly young tiger, steps out of a glowing open book into a Joseon-era royal courtyard with wooden halls and curved tiled roofs; a kind king in royal robes stands on the stone steps.

scenes.narration_en: In those days, people spoke Korean, but they wrote with Chinese characters. Korean is different from Chinese, and the characters were hard to learn, so many ordinary people could not write down what they wanted to say.
scenes.illustration: A village lane: a farmer and a child look puzzled at a sheet covered with dense, abstract brush marks (unreadable squiggles, no real characters); Hoya scratches his head beside them.

scenes.narration_en: King Sejong felt sorry for them. So, in 1443, he himself created 28 new letters. Hoya's eyes go wide. "Brand-new letters for the sounds of Korean!"
scenes.illustration: King Sejong at a low wooden desk by lamplight, brush in hand; simple abstract strokes, dots and circles float above the paper like sparks (no readable letters); Hoya peeks over the desk edge.

scenes.narration_en: He named them Hunminjeongeum, "the proper sounds for teaching the people." An old-fashioned word for the people is baekseong. In his own words, he made the letters so people could learn them easily and use them every day.
scenes.gloss_en: "the proper sounds for teaching the people"
scenes.illustration: A sunny market street where a merchant, a grandmother and children each hold a small blank paper and smile; warm light suggests everyone can now write.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya practices a new phrase: "Baeugi swiwoyo, it's easy to learn!" Later, the scholar Jeong In-ji wrote that a wise person could understand the letters before a single morning was over.
scenes.illustration: Morning sun rising over palace roofs; Hoya sits cross-legged with a brush and blank paper, grinning proudly; a scholar in a black gat hat watches kindly.

scenes.narration_en: In 1446, a book named Hunminjeongeum was finished to explain the new letters. Scholars of the royal Hall of Worthies, Jiphyeonjeon, wrote its explanations and examples.
scenes.gloss_en: the Hall of Worthies (the king's hall of scholars)
scenes.illustration: Several scholars in Joseon robes working at desks in a quiet wooden hall, stacks of bound books with plain covers; one scholar holds up a finished book (cover blank, no text).

scenes.narration_en: Today we call these letters Hangeul. People in Korea read and write with them every day, and now you are learning them too!
scenes.illustration: Present-day scene: Hoya waves beside a child holding a pencil over a notebook (blank lines), with a modern Korean street softly behind them; no signs or readable text.

episodes.notes: Revised after two independent checks. 'Promulgation' wording removed from the narration and summary: the Sillok 1446/9 entry only records that Hunminjeongeum was completed ('是月, 訓民正音成'), and 국립국어원 says no official promulgation ceremony is recorded and that a September 1446 promulgation is unsupported; UNESCO, 국가유산포털 and 국립한글박물관 do use 'published/promulgated 1446', so f7 states both. Scene 2 now gives both reasons from Sejong's preface (Korean differs from Chinese; the characters were hard to learn). Scene 5 phrase fixed to 배우기 쉬워요 (baeugi swiwoyo, 'it's easy to learn'). The word 백성 now appears in scene 4 narration; scene 6 key word is 집현전. The 1443 and 1446 Sillok entries are month-end entries in the lunar calendar with no specific day (the 12th lunar month of Sejong 25 falls in early 1444 in the Gregorian calendar, but UNESCO, 국가유산포털 and encykorea all say 1443, so the story follows that convention). Scene 5 quotes only the first half of Jeong In-ji's line. The 'almost 600 years ago' wording is worked out from 1443. The companion 훈이 ('Sejong's cat' in BP04) was deliberately not used. Illustrations must not show a proclamation ceremony. Do not name a specific palace or a royal robe colour. f9: the 표준국어대사전 quotation could not be read (dynamic page) and was replaced by the UNESCO wording ('now called han-gul'); the 한국민족문화대백과사전 한글 entry also states the point. The 국가유산포털 description text quoted in f1, f7, f8 was re-read from the portal's description fragment (hub_img/html/cul_1111100700000) in the research folder. FINAL PASS (3rd check): scene 4 now says 'An old-fashioned word for the people is baekseong' and f4 cites 표준국어대사전 for 백성. All other facts re-verified unchanged.

episodes.summary_en: Hoya reads the 1446 Hunminjeongeum Haerye book and discovers that the five basic Hangeul consonants copy the shapes of the tongue, mouth, teeth and throat, while the basic vowels come from the sky, the earth and a person.
learning_goals: Describe how the five basic consonants ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ copy the shapes of the speech organs.
Explain that stronger sounds add a stroke (ㄴ → ㄷ → ㅌ).
Name the three basic vowel shapes · ㅡ ㅣ and what they copy (sky, earth, person).
Know that South Korea's spelling rules today count 24 basic letters (14 consonants, 10 vowels).
Read and say 입, 목구멍, 하늘, 땅, 사람, 자음 and 모음 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya finds a very special old book: the Hunminjeongeum Haerye edition from 1446. Haerye means explanations and examples. Inside, scholars explained how the letters were designed!
scenes.gloss_en: the Haerye edition (the book with explanations and examples)
scenes.illustration: Hoya gently opens an old string-bound book with yellowed pages on a low table; soft light glows from the pages (pages shown as faint lines, no readable text).

scenes.narration_en: Secret number one: the five basic consonants copy the shapes of the parts of the body we speak with. The old book says the letter ㄱ copies the root of the tongue closing the throat. Hoya points at the picture.
scenes.gloss_en: giyeok, the letter for the g/k sound
scenes.illustration: Simple friendly side-view diagram of a head with the root of the tongue closing the throat, drawn in soft colors, as the old book describes; Hoya points at it with his tail. The app overlays the letter; no text in the image.

scenes.narration_en: Now ㄴ. The old book says it copies the tongue touching the upper gum. And ㅁ copies the shape of the mouth. Hoya opens wide: "Ip!" That means mouth.
scenes.illustration: Two small side-view diagrams: a tongue touching the upper gum, and a square-ish open mouth; Hoya opens his mouth wide in a funny face. No text in the image.

scenes.narration_en: ㅅ is shaped like a tooth, and ㅇ is shaped like the throat. So the five basic consonants, ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ, each copy a part of the body that makes the sound.
scenes.illustration: A playful row of five simple body-part icons (tongue root, tongue tip, mouth, tooth, round throat) like stepping stones, with Hoya hopping across them. No letters drawn.

scenes.narration_en: Secret number two: when a sound is stronger, add a stroke! ㄴ gets one more line and becomes ㄷ, and one more line makes ㅌ. Hoya draws them in the air with his tail.
scenes.illustration: Hoya swishes his tail through the air leaving three glowing ribbon trails that grow from one bend to more lines (abstract ribbons; the app overlays ㄴ ㄷ ㅌ).

scenes.narration_en: Secret number three: the vowels. A round dot · copies the round sky, a flat line ㅡ copies the flat earth, and a standing line ㅣ copies a person standing up.

facts.claim_en: The five basic consonant letters ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅁ, ㅅ, ㅇ were made by copying the shapes of the speech organs used to pronounce each sound.

facts.claim_en: The three basic vowel letters copy heaven, earth and a person: · is round like heaven (the sky), ㅡ is flat like the earth, and ㅣ stands upright like a person.

sources.quote_or_locator: "'ㅗ'는 'ㆍ'와 'ㅡ'가 어울려서 이루어진 모양이며, 'ㅏ'는 'ㅣ'와 'ㆍ' … 가 어울려서 이루어진 것이다."

facts.claim_en: Hunminjeongeum began with 28 letters. Some of them, such as ㆆ, ㅿ and ·, are no longer used, and the current South Korean spelling rules (Hangeul Matchumbeop) set 24 basic letters: 14 consonants and 10 vowels. (North Korea's norms count 40 letters, because they also count double consonants and compound vowels.)

episodes.notes: The letter-shape explanations follow the Haerye's 'Jejahae' (제자해) as summarized by 한국민족문화대백과사전. The Haerye's yin-yang and five-elements philosophy is left out as too advanced. The add-a-stroke rule has exceptions (ㆁ, ㄹ, ㅿ, per 한국민족문화대백과사전), so the narration gives only the ㄴ→ㄷ→ㅌ example. The narration says 'a few old ones are no longer used' rather than naming exactly four, because ㆁ merged with ㅇ rather than disappearing. The 국립국어원 essay (004d/004g) notes that a few details of the design principle are still debated among scholars; the story keeps to the consensus points. Because illustrations must contain no text, the app should overlay the jamo (ㄱ, ㄴ, ㅏ and so on) as UI text on the scene art. REVISED: the shape descriptions now follow the Haerye wording exactly (ㄱ = root of the tongue closing the throat, 象舌根閉喉之形; ㄴ = tongue touching the upper gum, 象舌附上腭之形) and no longer promise a physical sensation or add modern phonetics ('back of the tongue blocks the throat', 'ridge behind the upper teeth' removed; narration and illustration). The summary now says 'five basic consonants' (only ㄱ ㄴ ㅁ ㅅ ㅇ copy speech organs; others add strokes). Scene 2 no longer lists 'lips' (the Haerye names tongue root, tongue, mouth, tooth, throat). Vocab 혀 removed because no scene shows it. FINAL PASS (3rd check): scene 8, goal 4 and f7 now say South Korea's spelling rules count 24 (North Korea's norms count 40). The ㄴ wording follows the standard Korean rendering of 象舌附上腭之形 ('tongue touching the upper gum'); the Chinese 上腭 literally means the upper palate/jaw, so no finer anatomical claim is made.

episodes.summary_en: Hoya finds out why South Korea celebrates Hangeul Day on October 9: it is based on a date written at the end of the 1446 Haerye book, which was found around 1940. The day began as 'Gagyanal' in 1926.
learning_goals: Know that Hangeul Day (한글날) is October 9 in South Korea.
Explain that the date was set using the date written at the end of the Hunminjeongeum Haerye book (a lunar-calendar date), converted to the solar calendar.
Know that the Haerye book is a National Treasure and was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 1997.
Read and say 한글날, 음력, 10월 9일, 국보 and 고마워요 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: October 9 is Hangeullal, Hangeul Day! South Korea celebrates King Sejong's letters on this day. It became a national day in 2005 and a public holiday again in 2013. North Korea marks its own day on January 15.
scenes.illustration: A bright autumn day: families in a park, children holding blank paper fans and colorful streamers; Hoya waves a small flag with only a simple circle pattern. No text or signs.

scenes.narration_en: Why October 9? Hoya opens the Haerye book once more. At the very end, a note by Jeong In-ji gives a date: the first ten days of the ninth month of 1446, by the lunar calendar.
scenes.illustration: Close-up of Hoya's paw beside the last page of an old string-bound book (lines only, no readable text); a crescent moon glows softly in the window.

scenes.narration_en: People took the last of those ten days and converted it to the solar calendar. By the method they used, that gave October 9! Hoya stamps the date on his calendar with a paw print.
scenes.illustration: A wall calendar page with blank squares; one square gets a big orange paw print from Hoya; a moon on one side and a sun on the other suggest lunar and solar calendars. No numbers or text.

scenes.narration_en: Around 1940, an original copy of this book was found in an old house in Andong. The old royal records had only said the book was finished "this month". Today the book is kept by the Kansong Art Museum.
scenes.illustration: An old wooden hanok room with a carefully wrapped bundle of silk and paper being opened by gentle hands, revealing an old book; Hoya watches with wide eyes.

scenes.narration_en: This book is a National Treasure of Korea. In 1997, UNESCO added it to the Memory of the World Register, which honors documents that matter to the whole world.
scenes.illustration: The old book resting in a glass museum case under soft light; Hoya and a child look at it respectfully from behind a low rope. No labels or text.

scenes.narration_en: The very first celebration was held in 1926. It was called Gagyanal, a name said to come from how people practiced syllables: ga, gya, geo, gyeo. In 1928, it became Hangeullal.
scenes.gloss_en: Gagya Day (the first name of Hangeul Day)
scenes.illustration: A 1920s-style gathering in a simple hall: people in hanbok and early modern clothes clapping; Hoya in the front row, smiling. No banners or text.

scenes.narration_en: Hangeul's story reaches the whole world. UNESCO even gives a literacy prize named after King Sejong. Hoya bows deeply: "Gomawoyo, Sejong Daewangnim! Thank you, King Sejong!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya bowing politely toward a warm sunrise, with children from many backgrounds holding open books with blank pages around him.

facts.claim_en: The end of the Haerye book carries Jeong In-ji's date: the first ten days (sanghan) of the 9th month of 1446, by the lunar calendar. Hangeul Day was set by taking the last of those days, the 10th day of the 9th lunar month, and converting it to the solar (yangnyeok) calendar; by the method used when the day was set, this gives October 9. (From 1932 to 1945, observances that assumed the end of the 9th lunar month fell on October 29 and then October 28, before the day was moved to October 9.)
facts.claim_ko: 해례본 끝 정인지의 글에는 '정통 11년(1446) 9월 상한'이라는 날짜가 적혀 있다. 한글날은 상한(초하루~초열흘)의 마지막 날인 음력 9월 10일을 양력으로 환산하여 정해졌으며, 한글날을 정할 때 쓴 방법으로는 10월 9일이 된다. (1932년부터 1945년까지는 음력 9월 그믐으로 가정하여 양력 10월 29일, 이어서 10월 28일에 기념하다가 10월 9일로 바뀌었다.)

episodes.notes: REVISED. (1) The narration no longer says the date conversion is settled: it says People converted the last of the ten days to the solar calendar and 'by the method they used' got October 9. The conversion method is not treated as settled: earlier observances (which assumed the last day of the lunar 9th month) used Oct 29, then Oct 28, before Oct 9 was adopted (encykorea E0061511, 국립국어원 origin/001); one fact-checker also found press commentary arguing that Oct 9 does not match a strict Julian or Gregorian conversion (low-authority sources, not re-verified here). f3 records the first point and the narration says only 'by the method they used'. (2) 'Korea celebrates' -> 'South Korea celebrates'; North Korea's January 15 (조선글날) is stated in scene 1 (f10, sourced to 국립국어원 KTV programme and 서울신문 1990). Caveat: the 국립한글박물관 webzine 59 calls one theory about how that North Korean date is derived 'unconfirmed' (확인되지 않은 것), so the story states only that the day is marked on January 15, not how it was derived. (3) 'Kansong Art Museum in Seoul' -> 'kept by the Kansong Art Museum': in 2024 the book travelled to the new Kansong Art Museum in Daegu for its opening show (서울신문 2024-05-08), and UNESCO gives no city. RR would be 'Gansong'; the museum's own English spelling 'Kansong' (used by UNESCO) is kept. (4) Scene 4 no longer says 'nobody knew the exact day'. The sources disagree on when October 9 was first celebrated (1945 according to 국립한글박물관, 1946 according to 한국민족문화대백과사전), so no year is given. 'Said to' in scene 6 hedges the 'ga-gya-geo-gyeo' origin, as the museum itself reports it as hearsay. The second, privately held Haerye copy (the 'Sangju copy') is left out because its status is unresolved. The purchase by Jeon Hyeong-pil is left out for brevity. The founding year of the King Sejong Literacy Prize (1989) is on the UNESCO page only, so the narration does not give it. The UNESCO 'country overview' source in f7 was dropped because its page could not be loaded. The official title in the heritage register is simply 'Hunminjeongeum' (국보 훈민정음). Fact f3 also names the Gregorian calendar (second-checker request); the narration keeps the simpler 'solar calendar'. FINAL PASS (3rd check): f3 no longer says 'Gregorian' because no cited source states the calendar used for the October 9 conversion (encykorea: 1932-33 Julian -> Oct 29, 1934-45 Gregorian -> Oct 28; 국립국어원: Oct 9 = Oct 29 minus about 20 days). f10 now has three sources. Book location: 국가유산포털 still lists Seoul (성북동), while the book was shown at the new Kansong Art Museum in Daegu in autumn 2024; the story only says 'kept by the Kansong Art Museum' (UNESCO wording).

episodes.summary_en: Hoya visits Heungdeoksa Temple in Cheongju, where Jikji was printed with metal movable type in 1377. It is the world's oldest surviving book of its kind, and its one remaining volume is kept in Paris.
learning_goals: Explain in one sentence what movable metal type is.
Know that Jikji was printed in 1377 at Heungdeoksa Temple in Cheongju and is the world's oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type.
Know where the surviving volume is kept today (the National Library of France) and that it was inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2001.
Read and say 절, 스님, 제자, 활자, 금속활자 and 박물관 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya travels to Cheongju in the time of the Goryeo kingdom. At Heungdeoksa Temple, people are busy with something amazing: printing a book with letters made of metal!
scenes.illustration: A peaceful Goryeo-era temple courtyard with a wooden hall and a stone pagoda; inside an open door, figures bend over a work table with small shiny pieces. Hoya peeks around a pillar.

scenes.narration_en: The book is called Jikji. In 1372, a wise old monk named Baegun, then 75 years old, gathered important teachings of the Buddha and great teachers into it.
scenes.illustration: An elderly monk in gray robes writing calmly with a brush at a low desk by a paper window; mountains outside. No readable text on the paper.

scenes.narration_en: In 1377, Baegun's students printed the book here, with support from a Buddhist nun named Myodeok.
scenes.illustration: Two younger monks carefully lifting a freshly printed sheet (shown as soft gray lines, no readable text) while a nun in robes watches kindly.

scenes.narration_en: How does it work? Each character is its own little piece of metal type. Printers line the pieces up to make a page, then print it. Metal type made printing handier and mistakes easier to fix.
scenes.gloss_en: printing type (one piece for each character)
scenes.illustration: Close-up of hands placing tiny metal blocks into a tray frame in neat rows (block faces shown blank or as abstract bumps); Hoya holds one tiny block up to the light.

scenes.narration_en: Jikji is the oldest surviving book in the world printed with movable metal type. Old records show metal type was used in Goryeo even earlier, but Jikji is the oldest such book that still exists.
scenes.illustration: Hoya proudly holds up an old bound book like a trophy on a small hill, with a gentle golden glow behind him; the cover is plain.

scenes.narration_en: The book had two volumes. Only the second volume survives today, and it is kept at the National Library of France in Paris.
scenes.gloss_en: the second (last) volume of a set
scenes.illustration: A quiet, grand library reading room with tall shelves and arched windows; one old book rests safely in a protective case. No signs, no flags, no text.

scenes.narration_en: In 2001, UNESCO added Jikji to the Memory of the World Register. UNESCO also has a prize carrying its name, for people who help protect old documents and share them.
scenes.illustration: Hoya and children around the world holding hands in a circle around a glowing old book floating above a globe. No text.

scenes.narration_en: Heungdeoksa seems to have been lost in a fire long ago. But in 1985, archaeologists digging at the site found a metal piece carved with the name Heungdeoksa, so its site was confirmed. Today the Cheongju Early Printing Museum stands beside it.
scenes.illustration: Present day: a grassy temple site with stone foundations and a rebuilt hall, and a modern museum building nearby; Hoya waves to visiting families. No signs or text.

episodes.summary_en: At Haeinsa Temple, Hoya discovers the Tripitaka Koreana: more than 80,000 woodblocks of Buddhist scriptures carved between 1237 and 1248, still kept safe today.
learning_goals: Know that the Tripitaka Koreana (Palman Daejanggyeong) is a set of more than 80,000 woodblocks of Buddhist scriptures carved in Goryeo between 1237 and 1248.
Explain why the blocks were carved: a wish for the Buddha's protection during the Mongol invasions.
Know that the woodblocks are kept at Haeinsa Temple and were inscribed on UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2007.
Read and say 해인사, 대장경, 팔만, 나무, 경판 and 글자 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya climbs Gayasan Mountain to Haeinsa Temple in Hapcheon. Peeking through the slats of a long wooden hall, he gasps. Shelves of carved wooden blocks stretch on, row after row!
scenes.illustration: Hoya on a forest path up a green mountain toward a temple with tiled roofs; inset: a long dim hall with tall wooden shelves packed with dark wooden blocks seen through vertical window slats.

scenes.narration_en: These are the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks. In Korean they are called Daejanggyeong, which means a complete collection of Buddhist scriptures.
scenes.gloss_en: the complete collection of Buddhist scriptures (Tripitaka)
scenes.illustration: Rows of wooden printing blocks on shelves, each with small end pieces; warm light falls across them; Hoya stands small and amazed in the aisle. Block faces shown as texture, no readable characters.

scenes.narration_en: They were carved in the Goryeo kingdom, from 1237 to 1248. Mongol armies had invaded the land, and people carved the scriptures hoping the Buddha's power would protect their country.
scenes.gloss_en: Goryeo, the Korean kingdom of that time
scenes.illustration: Calm workshop scene: carvers in Goryeo clothing bent over wooden boards with small knives, focused and peaceful; distant mountains outside. No fighting, no soldiers.

scenes.narration_en: There are more than 80,000 blocks, which is one reason people call them Palman Daejanggyeong. Palman means eighty thousand! Hoya starts counting, then laughs. "That would take me all year!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya sitting on the floor counting on his paws, dizzy little stars circling his head, with endless shelves of blocks behind him.

scenes.narration_en: Each block, a gyeongpan, is carved on both sides. Most are made of wild cherry wood, coated with lacquer to protect them, and fitted with metal plates at the corners.
scenes.illustration: A single woodblock shown large, tilted to reveal both carved faces as abstract texture, dark lacquer sheen, and small metal plates at the four corners; a cherry tree in blossom behind it.

scenes.narration_en: Carvers cut tens of millions of characters into the wood, all neat and even, as if one hand had carved them all. Scholars around the world praise how accurate they are.
scenes.illustration: Close-up of a carver's steady hands and a small knife over a board covered in tiny, even raised marks (abstract pattern, not real characters); Hoya watches, holding his breath.

scenes.narration_en: Today the woodblocks are a National Treasure of Korea. In 2007, UNESCO added them to the Memory of the World Register.
scenes.illustration: Hoya proudly standing beside a single woodblock displayed on a cushion, with a soft starburst behind it suggesting world recognition. No logos or text.

scenes.narration_en: Almost 800 years later, the blocks are still kept safe at Haeinsa. Hoya whispers, "Sojunghaeyo, they're precious." Next time, let's find out how the buildings protect them!
scenes.illustration: Evening at Haeinsa: the long storage halls glowing softly at the top of the temple grounds under a starry sky; Hoya sits quietly on the steps.

facts.claim_en: There are more than 80,000 blocks. UNESCO's Memory of the World record gives 81,258; the Korea Heritage Service notes that this figure comes from a survey made under Japanese rule and includes some blocks re-carved in Joseon. This is one reason the set is called Palman ('eighty thousand') Daejanggyeong; the name is also linked to the 84,000 teachings (beopmun) the blocks are said to contain.

episodes.reference_display: Sources: 국가유산청 국가유산포털; 한국민족문화대백과사전; UNESCO Memory of the World; UNESCO World Heritage Centre
episodes.notes: The carving period follows 국가유산포털, 한국민족문화대백과사전 and UNESCO WHC (1237–1248). Some accounts count the whole project, preparation included, as about 16 years ending in 1251, so the narration gives only 1237–1248. The count of 81,258 comes from a survey made under Japanese rule and includes some blocks re-carved in Joseon (국가유산포털), so the narration says 'more than 80,000'. Where the carving took place (Ganghwa versus Namhae) is treated differently across sources and is left out. The 1398 move to Haeinsa appears only on 국가유산포털 pages, so it is left out too. The earlier set of blocks lost to fire in 1232 is left out to keep the war content mild. UNESCO's Memory of the World page places Haeinsa in the 'southwest' of the peninsula, but Haeinsa is in South Gyeongsang Province in the southeast, so that phrase was not used. 'Almost 800 years later' is worked out from 1248. The official heritage name is 합천 해인사 대장경판 (Hapcheon Haeinsa Daejanggyeongpan). REVISED: scene 1 no longer puts Hoya 'inside' the hall (visitor entry is restricted, see story-janggyeong-panjeon). f5 attributes the exact figure 81,258 to UNESCO (verified on the Memory of the World page) and records the Korea Heritage Service caveat; other published counts (about 81,350; 81,352) were reported by one fact-checker but not verified here, so no exact number appears in the narration. Second sources added for lacquer (f6) and the tens of millions of characters (f7: 5,200여 만자, 국가유산포털). The wild-cherry wood and corner metal plates (f6) still rest on one authoritative source (한국민족문화대백과사전; spelled 산벗나무 there). The UNESCO WHC page blocks automated access; its text was re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot. Vocab 새기다 dropped and 경판 added to scene 5 so every vocab word appears in a scene. FINAL PASS (3rd check): wild cherry wood (about 64-70% of blocks) and corner metal plates (copper) now rest on three sources (한국민족문화대백과사전, 정책브리핑, 박상진 study). The purpose of the lacquer is stated by 한국민족문화대백과사전 and the 국가유산포털 MoW page (preserves the carving); 박상진 doubts its protective effect, so treat 'to protect them' as the official wording.

episodes.summary_en: Hoya explores Janggyeong Panjeon, the 15th-century halls at Haeinsa whose clever windows and layered floors have protected the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks for some 500 years.
learning_goals: Know that Janggyeong Panjeon at Haeinsa Temple was built to store the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks and dates from the 15th century.
Explain two design features that protect the woodblocks: windows of different sizes for airflow, and a floor layered with charcoal, lime, salt and sand to control moisture.
Know that Janggyeong Panjeon was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1995.
Read and say 건물, 창문, 숯, 바람 and 지켜요 with romanization.

scenes.narration_en: Hoya returns to Haeinsa and climbs to the highest part of the temple grounds. Here stand the Janggyeong Panjeon, the halls made to store the woodblocks. They are the oldest buildings still standing at Haeinsa.
scenes.gloss_en: Janggyeong Panjeon, the woodblock storage halls at Haeinsa
scenes.illustration: Hoya climbing stone stairs to a terrace at the top of a mountain temple; two long, plain wooden halls with tiled roofs stand side by side above the other temple roofs.

scenes.narration_en: Two long halls stand side by side: Sudarajang in the south and Beopbojeon in the north. Two small buildings sit at the ends, so together they form a rectangle around a courtyard.
scenes.illustration: Bird's-eye view of four plain wooden buildings forming a rectangle around a sandy courtyard, two long and two short; Hoya waves from the courtyard.

scenes.narration_en: These halls were built in the 15th century, during the Joseon dynasty. There are no fancy decorations. Every part was designed for one job: keeping the woodblocks safe.
scenes.gloss_en: Joseon, the Korean dynasty of that time
scenes.illustration: Front view of a long, simple wooden hall with unpainted pillars and rows of slatted windows; Hoya points out how plain and tidy it looks.

scenes.narration_en: Look at the windows! The windows on the front and back walls are different sizes, and the upper and lower windows differ too. This helps the wind flow through the halls.
scenes.illustration: Cutaway side view of a hall: slatted windows of different sizes high and low on opposite walls, with gentle curved arrows of breeze flowing through past the shelves; Hoya's fur ruffles in the wind.

scenes.narration_en: Now look down. Under the earthen floor are layers of charcoal, lime and salt with sand. They soak up extra moisture when the air is damp and give it back when it is dry.
scenes.illustration: Cross-section of the ground under a hall showing simple colored layers (black charcoal, white lime, pale salt, tan sand) beneath an earthen floor; Hoya kneels, peering at the layers.

scenes.narration_en: Wind, sunlight and earth work together. Thanks to this natural design, the woodblocks have stayed safe from damp, mice and insects for some 500 years.
scenes.illustration: Sunlight streaming through slatted windows onto rows of woodblocks; a small mouse and a beetle turn away outside the wall while a breeze swirls leaves; Hoya smiles.

scenes.narration_en: In 1995, UNESCO added Janggyeong Panjeon to the World Heritage List. UNESCO calls it the oldest depository of the Tripitaka, the Buddhist scriptures.
scenes.illustration: The two long halls under a clear autumn sky with colorful maple leaves on the mountain; a soft glowing outline around the buildings suggests special recognition. No logos or text.

scenes.narration_en: To help keep the temperature and humidity steady, visitor entry is restricted. Hoya peeks through the window slats and whispers, "Uriga jikyeoyo, we protect it together!"
scenes.illustration: Hoya and a child quietly peeking through vertical window slats from outside, careful not to touch; inside, shelves of woodblocks rest in calm shadow.

episodes.notes: Theme is set to 'crafts' because the episode is about building and conservation design; switch it to 'letters' if the cluster should stay in one theme. The original construction date is unknown (국가유산포털), so the narration says '15th century' (UNESCO WHC, 국가유산포털). The sources consulted do not say which wall or row has the larger windows, so the narration only says the sizes differ, and illustrations should not suggest a specific pattern. 국가유산포털 also calls it the 'world's only building for storing Tripitaka woodblocks'; the narration uses UNESCO's more conservative wording, 'oldest depository of the Tripitaka', instead. The building's survival through the 1592 war is left out, because the story avoids war content. The visitor-entry restriction is as stated on the WHC page on the access date; rules may change. The official heritage name is 합천 해인사 장경판전 (National Treasure, designated 1962). REVISED: 'oldest buildings' -> 'oldest buildings still standing at Haeinsa' (국가유산포털: 해인사에 남아있는 건물 중 가장 오래 되었다; verified in the portal's description text and its UNESCO page). Visitor restriction (f9): the UNESCO WHC text, re-read on an Internet Archive snapshot, says restrictions exist 'in order to control the temperature and humidity within the depositories'; the fire-protection measures on the same page (guards, surveillance, lightning rod) are a separate sentence. Narration now says visitors 'cannot walk inside' to match the UNESCO wording, and the old 'to keep the air just right inside' phrase was replaced. Only UNESCO is cited for this restriction; no 국가유산청 page with it was found, and rules may change. Check distractors replaced with plausible wrong answers. Vocab 소금/습기 dropped (not shown in a scene) and 세계유산 added. FINAL PASS (3rd check): scene 8 now says 'visitor entry is restricted' (UNESCO wording) instead of 'visitors cannot walk inside', because Haeinsa runs pre-booked guided tours inside Beopbojeon (since 2021-06, 경향신문). Current rules should be checked on haeinsa.or.kr before any release.
